title: JavaScript properly: values, types and variables
goal: Understand JavaScript's basic types and variables well enough to predict what simple code prints.

concepts: Running JS: node file.js, the browser console, and <script src defer>
let vs const (and why to avoid var)
Primitive types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined (and bigint, symbol exist)
typeof and its quirks (typeof null is 'object')
Template literals: `Hello ${name}`
Type conversion: Number('42'), String(42), and surprises like '5' + 1

build.task: In day25/, write profile-card.js that runs with node. Store your name, age, city, isStudent and a skills count in well-named const/let variables. Print a formatted profile card using template literals (multi-line). Then write conversions.js that prints the result and typeof for at least 10 expressions you predicted first (e.g. '5' + 1, '5' - 1, Number(''), Number('abc'), true + 1, null + 1, undefined + 1). Write your prediction as a comment next to each line BEFORE running.

starterFiles.name: day25/conversions.js

acceptance: profile-card.js runs with node and prints a multi-line card using template literals
const is used for values that never change, let only where they do; no var
conversions.js has at least 10 expressions, each with a prediction comment written before running
Every wrong prediction has a one-line explanation

hints: Multi-line template literal: const card = `Name: ${name}\nCity: ${city}`; or just press Enter inside the backticks.
+ with a string anywhere does string concatenation. -, *, / always try to convert to numbers.
Number('') is 0, Number('abc') is NaN, null becomes 0 in maths, undefined becomes NaN.

explainBack.q: Pick one prediction you got wrong. Explain what JavaScript actually did.
lookFor: e.g. + concatenates with strings, - converts to number

explainBack.q: When do you use const and when let? Show an example from your code.
lookFor: const objects can still be mutated (bonus)

lastHintExplanation: The + operator concatenates if either side is a string, so '5' + 1 is '51'. Other arithmetic operators convert both sides to numbers, so '5' - 1 is 4. null converts to 0 and undefined to NaN. Use const by default and let only when the variable must be reassigned.

predict.why: A historical bug in JavaScript: typeof null is 'object'.

dsa.note: You now know more JS. Solve these with clear variable names and a comment explaining the idea.

title: Operators, comparisons and conditions
goal: Write branching logic correctly, including the traps of == vs === and truthy/falsy values.

concepts: Arithmetic, assignment, increment, % (remainder)
Comparison: === and !== (use these), why == is risky
Truthy and falsy values: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN
Logical operators &&, ||, ! and short-circuiting
?? (nullish coalescing) vs ||
if / else if / else, ternary ?:, and switch

build.task: In day26/, write grades.js: a function-free script (functions come Day 28) that, for a hard-coded array of 6 students' marks, prints each student's grade (A ≥ 90, B ≥ 75, C ≥ 60, D ≥ 40, F below 40), whether they passed, and a special message using a switch for grade A and F. Then write shipping.js that calculates delivery cost from variables weightKg, isPrime, pincode and couponCode: free for Prime orders above 0.5 kg... design your own clear rules (at least 4) and write them as a comment at the top. Use ?? for a default couponCode.
acceptance: Only === / !== used, never == or !=
Grade boundaries correct (test 90, 89, 75, 40, 39)
A switch handles at least two grade cases
shipping.js lists its rules in a comment and every rule is reachable
?? used for a default value and you can explain why || would differ

hints: Check the highest grade first: if (m >= 90) ... else if (m >= 75) .... Otherwise 95 would match '>= 40' first.
Test boundary values on purpose. Bugs live at 89/90, not at 50.
couponCode ?? 'NONE' replaces only null/undefined. couponCode || 'NONE' would also replace an empty string ''.

explainBack.q: Why should you use === instead of ==? Give an example where == surprises you.
lookFor: example like 0 == '' is true or '1' == 1 is true

explainBack.q: Explain the difference between ?? and || using your couponCode.
Why does the order of your if/else if conditions matter?
lookFor: first true branch runs and the rest are skipped

lastHintExplanation: == converts types before comparing (0 == '' is true), which hides bugs; === requires the same type and value. || falls back on any falsy value (0, '', false, null, undefined, NaN) while ?? falls back only on null or undefined. In an if/else if chain the first true condition wins, so check the strictest threshold first.

predict.why: || skips falsy 0; ?? keeps 0 because it's not null/undefined.
'0' is a non-empty string, which is truthy.

title: Loops in practice: a number guessing game
goal: Use loops, break/continue and conditions together to build a small interactive game in the browser.

concepts: for, while, do...while and when to use each
for...of over arrays and strings
break and continue
Math.random(), Math.floor() for random integers in a range
prompt(), alert() and console.log for quick browser interaction
Avoiding infinite loops

build.task: In day27/, build a number guessing game that runs in the browser (index.html loads game.js). The computer picks a random integer 1–100. The player has 7 tries using prompt(). After each guess say 'higher' or 'lower'; handle Cancel (null) by ending the game, and handle non-numbers by not counting the try. At the end, show the result and the list of guesses. Ask 'Play again?' with confirm(). Also write patterns.js (node) that prints a right-angle triangle and a multiplication table 1–10 using nested loops.
acceptance: Random number is always an integer between 1 and 100 inclusive
At most 7 counted tries; invalid input doesn't use up a try
Pressing Cancel ends the game cleanly
Shows all guesses at the end and offers to play again
patterns.js prints a triangle and a 10×10 multiplication table with nested loops

hints: prompt returns a string, or null on Cancel. Check for null first, then convert with Number() and check Number.isNaN().
A while loop that counts tries: let tries = 0; while (tries < 7) { ... if (invalid) continue; tries++; ... if (correct) break; }.

explainBack.q: Show how your loop makes sure invalid input doesn't count as a try.
lookFor: or only increment on valid input

lastHintExplanation: Math.random() returns a number from 0 up to but not including 1. Multiplying by 100 gives 0–99.99…, Math.floor makes it 0–99, and +1 shifts the range to 1–100. Using continue before incrementing the counter skips invalid input without spending a try.

predict.q: for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i === 2) continue; if (i === 4) break; console.log(i) }
predict.why: 2 is skipped by continue; the loop stops at 4 before printing.

dsa.note: Look for a formula before writing a loop. Then check the formula with a loop.

questions.why: 10 men equal 16 women, so the team is 20 women. The job is 160 woman-days: 160/20 = 8.

Parameters, arguments, default parameters
return: a function without return gives undefined
Pure functions: same input, same output, no side effects
Functions as values: passing a function to another function (callbacks)

explainBack.q: What's the difference between a function that returns a value and one that prints it? Why did you return?
lookFor: return gives the value back to the caller
returned values can be tested and reused

explainBack.q: Explain what makes one of your utils functions pure.
lookFor: same input always gives same output
names their function (randomInt is not pure)

lastHintExplanation: A function that returns a value hands it back to its caller, who can test it, store it or pass it on. One that only prints has a side effect and returns undefined. A pure function always gives the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself, which makes it easy to test. randomInt is not pure because its output varies.

predict.q: function add(a, b) { a + b } console.log(add(2, 3))
predict.why: No return statement, so the function returns undefined.
Defaults apply only for undefined, not null.

title: Scope, hoisting and closures
goal: Predict which variables a function can see, and use closures to keep private state.

concepts: Global, function and block scope (let/const are block-scoped)
The scope chain: inner functions see outer variables
Hoisting: function declarations vs let/const (temporal dead zone)
Closures: a function remembers the variables where it was created
Using closures for private state: counters, once(), simple caches
The classic var-in-a-loop bug

build.task: In day29/, write closures.js with: (1) createCounter(start = 0) returning { increment, decrement, reset, value } where the count can't be changed from outside; (2) once(fn) that lets fn run only the first time; (3) makeMultiplier(n) returning a function; (4) createBankAccount(owner) with deposit, withdraw (refuse if not enough balance) and getHistory. Use your check() helper for at least 12 checks. Finally write scope-puzzles.js: 5 short snippets about scope/hoisting with your prediction comment, then the actual output.
acceptance: counter's count can't be read or changed except via its functions (no property holding it)
once(fn) returns the first result on later calls without running fn again
Bank account refuses to overdraw and records every transaction in history
At least 12 passing checks
scope-puzzles.js has 5 snippets with predictions and actual results, including the var-in-loop case

hints: Private state: declare let count inside createCounter, and return an object of functions that use it. Nothing outside can reach count directly.
once: keep let called = false and let result inside; on the first call set both, then always return result.
var-in-loop: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)) prints 3 3 3. Try it with let and explain the difference.

explainBack.q: Explain how your counter keeps count private. Where does count live after createCounter returns?
lookFor: nothing outside can access it directly

explainBack.q: Why does the var loop print 3 3 3 but let prints 0 1 2?
lookFor: var is function-scoped: one shared i
let creates a new binding per iteration
callbacks run after the loop finishes

lastHintExplanation: A closure is a function plus the variables it could see when it was created. createCounter's local count stays alive because the returned functions still reference it, but nothing else can reach it. With var there is one i shared by every iteration, so callbacks that run later all see its final value; let creates a fresh i for each iteration.

predict.why: let is hoisted but in the temporal dead zone until its declaration runs.
Function declarations are fully hoisted, so they can be called before the line they're written on.

console.log with labels; console.table for arrays of objects
The debugger statement and breakpoints in Chrome DevTools or VS Code
Stepping: step over, step into, watch variables
Common JS bugs: missing return, off-by-one, = vs ===, wrong starting value

build.task: Copy the starter into day30/debug/cart.js and run it with node. It should print Total ₹1130.00, With SAVE10 ₹1017.00, With WRONG ₹1130.00 and Cheapest: Pen. It has 4 bugs. Find each one using console.log or a breakpoint (not by guessing), fix it, and commit each fix separately. Then add 6 checks with your check() helper so these bugs can't come back. Finish with day30/week5-notes.md: one confident topic and one weak topic for each of Days 25–29.

starterFiles.name: day30/debug/cart.js

acceptance: Output matches the 4 expected lines exactly
4 separate fix commits with messages naming each bug
6 checks added that would catch each bug
week5-notes.md has entries for Days 25–29

hints: First run shows a crash. Read the error: which line, and what was undefined? Then log what lineTotal returns.
Log i and items[i] inside the loop. Does the loop run one time too many?
In applyCoupon, a single = assigns, so the condition is always truthy. For cheapestItem, what's the first price that could ever be less than 0?
proof: Link to your final fix commit.

explainBack.q: Describe how you found the off-by-one bug. What did the log or debugger show?
lookFor: logged i / items[i] or used breakpoint

explainBack.q: Why did if (code = 'SAVE10') always run the discount?
lookFor: result of assignment is 'SAVE10', which is truthy

explainBack.q: What starting value should cheapestItem use and why?
lookFor: no price is below 0, so the original never changes

lastHintExplanation: Bug 1: lineTotal has no return, so it returns undefined and the total becomes NaN. Bug 2: i <= items.length reads items[3], which is undefined; use <. Bug 3: code = 'SAVE10' assigns, and the non-empty string is truthy, so every code gets the discount; use ===. Bug 4: cheapest starts at price 0, which no item beats; start from items[0] or Infinity.

predict.why: 0 + undefined is NaN, and NaN spreads through any later arithmetic.
